tasks.why: The engine evicted 8 running requests per 100 completed because the KV cache was full, so the KV cache is what binds. An FP8 KV cache stores about twice the tokens in the same memory on an H100, so it comes first. Capping concurrent requests below the 48 observed (to 32) stops the evictions at the cost of some queueing. Adding batch slots would make the evictions worse.

The same evictions as on the H100 task, on an AMD Instinct MI300X. CDNA 3 runs FP8 in hardware and the pinned vLLM 0.22.1 ROCm image supports an FP8 (e4m3) KV cache, so the FP8 KV cache still comes first and the sequence cap second. The plan is identical because the rules read the diagnosis, not the vendor. The AMD AITER kernels are not chosen: the diagnosis points at the KV cache or the queue, not at kernel time.

The KV cache was 97% full while six requests waited, so admission is limited by KV memory. The L40S is an Ada GPU with FP8 support, so an FP8 KV cache on the reviewed interactive profile is the change to measure. The engine did not report how many requests ran at once, so no running-request cap can be set and the plan records that. The reviewed balanced and throughput profiles are generic alternatives no rule chose, so they are left out.

Requests waited 640 ms at p95 inside the engine while the KV cache was only 41% used, so memory is not what holds them back; the scheduler admits too few per step. On an 80 GB H100, vLLM 0.22.1 already defaults to 1,024 sequences and 8,192 batched tokens, so the larger-batch setup raises both above those defaults (2,048 and 16,384) instead of restating them. Nothing points at precision or speculation.

RunPod's exact SKU name for the MI300X resolves to the reviewed 192 GB accelerator. vLLM 0.22.1 applies its 70 GB rule on ROCm too, so the defaults are already 1,024 sequences and 8,192 batched tokens, and the larger-batch setup raises them to 2,048 and 16,384. The small-memory values (512 and 8,192) would restate or lower the defaults and must not appear. The AMD AITER kernels are not chosen: the diagnosis points at the KV cache or the queue, not at kernel time.

The same queueing diagnosis on SGLang. SGLang sizes its batch limits from GPU memory when it starts, and InferCrane has not recorded that rule, so a larger-batch setup could equal the default. Rather than pay to measure a possible no-op, the plan records why and measures only the starting setup.

Requests waited while SMs had resident work on only 31% of cycles: the CPU side is not keeping the GPU fed. More API server processes take tokenization and HTTP handling off the engine's path, and streaming tokens in small groups cuts per-token work there. Both keep async scheduling and CUDA graphs on. vLLM already captures CUDA graphs by default, so no graph setup is added for a built-in runtime.

First tokens took 73% of p95 latency with 6,200-token prompts, so a per-step prompt budget of 16,384 tokens (twice the H100 default) finishes each prompt in fewer steps. Most requests share a system prompt, but vLLM 0.22.1 already caches prefixes by default and the starting setup keeps it on, so a prefix-cache setup would measure the starting setup twice; the plan records it as skipped instead.

82% of requests share a system prompt but only 9% of prompt tokens came from the cache. vLLM already caches prefixes by default and has no prefix-aware scheduling flag; routing requests that share a prompt to the same server is an endpoint change planned separately. Prompts average 700 tokens, too short for chunk size to matter. No flag change can address this, so only the starting setup is measured.

The same low reuse on SGLang. Its radix cache is on by default, but its default first-come-first-served schedule interleaves requests with different prompts; longest-prefix-match scheduling runs requests that share a prompt together so the prompt stays cached.

Recorded on 2026-11-17 (Qwen3-0.6B, one RTX 4090, replay at one request at a time): vLLM defaults served 246 tok/s, n-gram speculation 188 tok/s, and FP8 KV cache with 2048-token chunks 193 tok/s (2048 is already the default under 70 GiB, so that arm was FP8 KV alone). Both lost. With one request running, decode waits on weight reads, but speculation does not pay at 0.6B and lower weight precision is not proposed at 1.5B or fewer; the model also declares no prediction head and has no reviewed draft model or 4-bit checkpoint. Few requests run at once, so right-sizing the GPU is flagged for a separate run. Nothing is worth measuring, so only the starting setup is.

Same recorded workload seen from the gateway only, as on the real run, when the engine reported no metrics: first tokens took about half of p95 latency, but prompts average 278 tokens, far below any per-step prompt budget, so that time is not prompt work. No rule fires, so the planner proposes no change and asks for engine metrics instead of falling back to generic setups.

Decode took 85% of p95 latency with 64 requests running per server on 9,000-token contexts. Each step reads one copy of the weights but 64 long KV caches, so halving KV bytes with an FP8 KV cache comes first. For a throughput goal, larger batches share each weight read across more requests; FP8 weights are the weaker lever and follow. Rule set v5 also chooses speculation with the model's own prediction head in a decode-bound window, behind the FP8 KV cache at this load; this model's config declares no prediction head, so it is recorded as skipped and no setup applies it.

Decode-bound at 64 running requests, but on 1,500-token contexts and with no KV pressure. Below about 7k tokens of context BF16 KV has measured slightly better token latency, so an FP8 KV cache is not chosen. The goal is interactive, so larger batches, which raise latency, are not chosen either. FP8 weights remain. Rule set v5 chooses speculation with the model's own prediction head here too, and records it as skipped because this model's config declares no prediction head.

Decode took 85% of p95 latency with 12 requests running per server, above the low-concurrency limit of 4, on 3,000-token contexts, and the model's config declares a native prediction head. Each drafted token that is accepted saves a step, so speculation with three drafted tokens leads at up to 16 running requests; before rule set v5 only the low-concurrency rule chose it, so this window proposed no speculation at all. Larger batches and FP8 weights follow as in the other decode-bound plans, and the contexts are too short for an FP8 KV cache.

The long-context decode task with a model whose config declares a native prediction head. At 64 running requests on 9,000-token contexts the FP8 KV cache still comes first. Speculation is measured next: a drafted token is verified in the same step as every other request's tokens, so its gain shrinks as load rises, and above 16 running requests it is planned behind the FP8 KV cache and ahead of larger batches. The plan orders the measurement; it does not predict a gain at this load.

Two requests ran per server, so decode is bound by reading weights. FP8 weights quantized at load serve the same model files and halve those bytes. NVIDIA's reviewed NVFP4 checkpoint of this model would halve them again, but it serves different model files, and a campaign cannot rank setups that serve different files yet, so it is left out with that reason. No prediction head or draft model is declared, so speculation is recorded as skipped.

On the pinned SGLang image the starting setup is the image's untuned control, and the reviewed FP8 KV cache setup on the same image directly answers the evictions. The image's other setups (speculation, graph capture, prompt chunks) do not address KV capacity and are left out. Flag changes to a pinned image are not derived, so the running-request cap is recorded as skipped.

With 1.5 requests running per server, decode is bound by weight reads and the model declares a native prediction head, so the image's NEXTN speculation setups lead. They were also the measured winners on H200 in the recorded decode receipts. Speculation keeps async scheduling on in this family.

The window had too few fresh requests to diagnose. The planner must not guess a bottleneck or fall back to generic setups: it measures only the starting setup and asks for fresh traffic and engine metrics.
7% of requests failed. Speed comparisons on a failing endpoint are biased by the failures, so the planner adds no speed setups until the errors are fixed.

Decode dominates and the engine did not report concurrency, so the stage alone only weakly suggests FP8 weights. The GPU profile settles it: on 9,000-token contexts attention kernels took 56% of sampled GPU time against 31% for matrix multiplies, so the KV reads attention performs are the larger cost and an FP8 KV cache comes first. Speculation needs low concurrency, which was not reported, so it is not chosen.

The trace places the cost on the host: the GPU sat idle 29% of the window waiting on launches and 71% of kernels finished faster than their launch call. The levers for launch overhead are CUDA graphs and scheduling the next step while the GPU runs this one. vLLM 0.22.1 runs both by default, and under 70 GiB it captures graphs for batches up to 512 (min(256 x 2, 512)), far above the 6 requests running here, so a larger capture changes nothing. Decode-bound at 6 requests would choose FP8 weights, which are not proposed at 0.6B. No change is worth measuring, so only the starting setup is.

Requests waited while SMs had resident work on only 38% of cycles, and the trace names the cause: the GPU sat idle 24% of the window waiting on host launches, and 58% of kernels finished faster than their launch call. About 700 requests run per server, above the largest batch vLLM 0.22.1 captures a CUDA graph for on an 80 GB GPU (min(1024 x 2, 512) = 512), so those steps run without a full graph. Capturing graphs up to 880 (a quarter above 700, on vLLM's 16-step grid) addresses the measured cause and comes first. More API server processes and streaming tokens in small groups follow from the CPU-side finding. Async scheduling is already on by default, so it adds no setup.

Two GPUs per server, and the trace measured how much of their communication hides under compute: only 29%, leaving it holding the GPU 17% of the window with nothing running underneath. Spreading the model over more GPUs would add to that, so no wider layout is measured; fewer GPUs per server is the lever, and changing hardware is planned as a separate run. Decode is the bottleneck at 64 running requests on 1,500-token contexts with an interactive goal, which leaves FP8 weights.

Decode dominates and the engine did not report concurrency, so the stage alone only weakly suggests FP8 weights. The trace placed 74% of matrix-multiply time on the H100's roofline and found 90% of it below the ridge point: the multiplies wait on memory, not math. Smaller weights move fewer bytes per step, so FP8 weights come first with stronger support. 4-bit weights would need a publisher checkpoint a campaign cannot rank yet. Contexts are short, so an FP8 KV cache is not chosen.

The trace calls the matrix multiplies memory-bound, but it recorded shapes for only 18% of their time, so the verdict describes a small sample rather than the server. Idle time without a known cause and serving time the window cannot attribute name no change. Nothing is chosen until a trace with recorded shapes covers most of the multiply time.

On 9,000-token contexts the trace found attention taking 38% of kernel time, above its 35% threshold, so the KV reads attention performs are a large cost and an FP8 KV cache comes first. The trace's own finding replaces the coarser share rule for the same capture. Decode dominates with concurrency unreported, which weakly suggests FP8 weights next. Speculation needs low concurrency, which was not reported.

The H100 short-context decode task on an AMD Instinct MI300X. Writing answers is 85% of p95 request time, so the GPU's kernels are the work to speed up. vLLM 0.22.1 leaves AMD's AITER kernels off unless VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 (default False in vllm/envs.py; the pinned ROCm image does not set it), and AMD's vLLM optimization guide and the vLLM recipes' AMD preset both turn it on, so the AITER setup is measured first. It changes only that switch; FP8 weights follow as on the H100. FP8 KV cache and larger batches stay out for the same reasons as on the H100.

First tokens take 80% of p95 request time on 6,000-token prompts on an MI355X (CDNA 4, gfx950). Prompt processing is attention and matrix-multiply work, which AITER's kernels replace on this GPU and which vLLM 0.22.1 leaves off by default, so the AITER setup comes before the bigger prompt chunks the H100 long-prompt task chooses.

First tokens dominate, but prompts average 300 tokens, so first-token time is not prompt work and faster kernels for it are not the lever. Nothing is chosen on the MI300X either, and the plan asks for engine metrics.
The MI300X decode task on an H100. AITER is AMD's kernel library and no engine switch is reviewed for the CUDA platform, so the rule does not fire and the plan is the H100 plan.

The MI300X decode task on SGLang. SGLang's pinned ROCm image already sets SGLANG_USE_AITER=1 and no SGLang switch is reviewed, so the AITER rule has nothing to turn on and does not fire. FP8 weights remain, as for vLLM.
